hypothesis: Unmodified scaffold RandomForest establishes the starting RMSE for BEV.
observation: RMSE 0.013345 in 7.1s on 2017 Chevy Bolt data. Training finishes well under the 10-minute budget.
reasoning: With 8-9 minutes of budget unused, there is ample room to scale the model and add features. BEV energy is heavy-tailed (regen negatives), so tree-based non-parametric models should handle the distribution out of the box.

hypothesis: HGBR at defaults will beat RF(n=20, d=10) on BEV because GBMs handle heavy-tailed asymmetric targets better and are not capped at max_depth=10.
observation: RMSE 0.013347 in 4.6s - essentially tied with RF baseline (+0.015% worse, numerical noise). HGBR is ~35% faster to train, so there is headroom for more boosting iterations.
reasoning: HGBR defaults (max_iter=100) are under-parameterized relative to the baseline RF's effective capacity. The family swap alone does nothing - the value will come from scaling HGBR's iterations. Revert and retry with more capacity.

hypothesis: 10x more trees reduces forest variance and should cut RMSE meaningfully. At baseline's 7.1s, 200 trees should fit well within the 10-min budget.
observation: RMSE 0.013341 (-0.03%) in 23.5s. Improvement is tiny - 10x trees barely moved the needle. Linear scaling of train time confirms trees, not depth, is the bottleneck.
reasoning: Variance reduction from more trees has diminishing returns once n>=100. The next lever is bias: max_depth=10 likely caps expressivity with only 3 input features, and min_samples_split=10 limits leaf resolution. Try lifting depth/leaf constraints next.

hypothesis: Depth cap of 10 was limiting fit quality; uncapping lets trees express interaction structure and cut RMSE.
observation: RMSE 0.013964 (+4.7%) in 49.5s - clear overfit. Trees memorize the training distribution, including regen tail outliers that don't generalize.
reasoning: With only 3 input features and 160k+ rows, unlimited depth has no regularization so it memorizes noise. The BEV target has heavy regen tails that are per-sample outliers, not learnable structure. Moderate depth lift with leaf regularization is the right direction, not free depth.

hypothesis: Explicit v^2 gives trees a kinetic-energy nonlinearity without burning depth on approximation, should lower RMSE.
observation: RMSE 0.013341 - exactly tied with best (6-decimal match). Training 30.8s. Zero gain from the added feature.
reasoning: Trees partition speed_mph freely and can capture any monotone-in-v^2 split via speed_mph directly; v^2 adds no information a depth-10 forest cannot already express. Monotone transforms are redundant for trees. Future feature engineering should focus on INTERACTIONS (speed*grade, grade*miles) not monotone transforms of existing features.

description: add prev_speed_mph (previous-link speed, per-journey shift, fillna to self for first link)
hypothesis: Prior-link speed gives the model the vehicle's entry kinetic state, which determines how much of the current link's energy is accel/decel vs cruise. Particularly important for BEV where regen recovery on decel and accel cost are first-order terms.
observation: RMSE 0.009155 (-31.4%) in 29.1s. Massive gain from a single feature. This is the largest single-change improvement likely available.
reasoning: Link-independent features (speed, grade, miles) cannot distinguish a 30mph cruise from a 60->30 deceleration - same average speed, very different energy. Previous-link speed encodes the accel/decel direction and magnitude. This feature is available at inference (domain.md), so the win is real. Expect similar gains from other prev-link features (prev_grade, prev_miles, speed_delta).

hypothesis: Previous-link grade gives complementary state info (coasting from descent vs laboring from climb) that prev_speed alone does not encode.
observation: RMSE 0.009144 (-0.12%) in 35.8s. Small but real gain - much smaller than prev_speed.
reasoning: Prev_grade adds an independent dimension to vehicle-entry state but most of the information was already captured by prev_speed (since speed responds to grade). Marginal but worth keeping. Train time still well under budget.
